Q: Internal of .NET timer controller A:

The Windows Forms timer (System.Windows.Forms.Timer) will run on the UI thread (it will post timer events to the main event loop).

The System.Timers.Timer will by default use the thread pool for timer events.

To answer your updated question: Assuming you are using the System.Windows.Forms.Timer, the tick handler will always run to completion before the next tick event is run (since they always run on the same thread). Don't forget to wrap in try/finally though.

Q: How do I handle read system calls for HPC? A:

I concur with using the stdlib fgets()/sscanf() approach. (if you want to parse and read char-by-char with fgetc(), that's fine too) Regardless how you read you will have a BUFSIZ (8K on Linux) buffer filled by the system holding the data to be read. There is little benefit to altering the BUFSIZ argument (you are free to test). The compilers are excellent nowadays at optimizing your standard library code. As for using the data, depending on size, reading once into memory provides many benefits, from random access from that point forward to the ability to modify and write the entire file back out. If you don't need it all in memory, then just read, do you dry air calc and add the result to whatever statistic you are keeping, or just store the individual results in memory as needed.

As far as speed/efficiency goes, you will be hard pressed to write a routine using low-level read that will out perform what the compiler will do with standard library calls. Again, you are free to test a confirm for yourself. Even on an old spinning-rust Core2Duo, you can read the whole 300K line words file in a few milliseconds, so reads, even being the bottleneck, happen quite quickly. Good luck with your coding.
